en: A Concise Commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* Based on the Treatise of Bodhisattva Vasubandhu:
An Exegesis of the Meaning of the Qin Translation,
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhī'ēn of Chóngshèng Monastery in the Western Capital.
This sutra will now be explained through a fivefold analysis:
first, identifying the causes and conditions for the teaching;
second, determining the primary purpose of the sutra.
First, the assembly at the place of the three knowledges;
second, an account of the translation;
third, the formal explanation of the text’s meaning.
First, regarding the discernment of the causes and conditions for teaching,
there are ten points therein.
The first is for the purpose of proclaiming the bodhisattva practices.
As it is said in the sutra: "Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Noble sons and noble daughters who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
"One should abide thus and thus subdue one's mind," and so forth.
Second, because it accords with the teachings of all Buddhas, as the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One, [he has not]."
"The Tathāgata has nothing to say.
The commentary explains:
"The teachings of all Buddhas are termed 'no-teaching'."
Third, it is for the purpose of counteracting and eliminating attachment to a self and to phenomena.
As the Sūtra says: "If, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who hear this sūtra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it."
Such a person is indeed the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because this person has no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, and no notion of a life-span.

Why is this? The mark of a self is precisely no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are precisely no-marks. To explain: *Explanation:* This means that the conceptualization of a "self" is, in its true nature, devoid of any objective characteristic. Likewise, the conceptualizations of a "person," a "sentient being," and a "life-span" are likewise devoid of any objective characteristic. They are merely mental constructs arising from ignorance and attachment. Since these marks lack inherent existence, they are termed "no-marks. This teaching serves to dismantle the four types of grasping at a self, thereby leading one toward the realization of non-self (*anātman*). By understanding that these so-called "marks" are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature, one transcends all dualistic attachments. Thus, the text emphasizes that what appears as a substantial self or identity is, in fact, nothing more than a false appearance. This is the essential meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā teachings on emptiness.
In this text, why is it that at the beginning one counters the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*),
while later one counters the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*)?
It is because these four serve to sever both the seeds and the manifest forms of doubt.
Regarding the "planting of doubt," this refers to precluding it in the future, as in the sūtra:
"The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the marks of the body," and so forth, down to the later passage: "Do not entertain such thoughts."
The mention of "present doubt" is for the purpose of preventing its arising,
as in the sūtra where the Buddha tells Subhūti, "Do not speak thus," and so forth.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of generating inferential faith.
Regarding "inferential faith," as the sutra says:
"One should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas."
Regarding the phrase "Upon hearing these chapters and verses,
even for a single thought-moment, one gives rise to pure faith," and so forth:
this refers to what is called "attesting faith."
As the sutra says: "For what reason?
Because these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span;
they have neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas," and so forth.
Sixth, for the sake of accomplishing one's own benefit and the benefit of others.
Regarding "one's own benefit," as the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all signs."
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that "a bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving," and so forth.
Regarding "benefiting others," it is as the sutra says:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner."
...up to the point where the Tathāgata says, "All sentient beings are themselves non-sentient beings," and so forth.
Seventh, it is for the purpose of transforming and extinguishing heavy and light karmas, as the sutra states:
"Subhūti, if a good son or a good daughter..."
If one who upholds, recites, and studies this sutra is treated with contempt by others,
it is because of the karmic offenses committed in their previous lives.
They would have fallen into the evil realms;
however, because they are now treated with contempt by people of this world,
their karmic offenses from previous lives are thereby extinguished.
One shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Eighth, it is for the sake of liberating oneself from the afflictions of both seeing and cultivation;
as the Sūtra says: "At that time, I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span."
"Even when my body was being dismembered limb by limb in the past, if there had been any notion of a self,
a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span would have given rise to anger, resentment, and the like."
The ninth is for the purpose of demonstrating the causes of merit and wisdom.
As the sutra says: "Good sons and good daughters, suppose one were to give as an offering the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River."
If, moreover, there is a person who knows that all dharmas are without self and thereby achieves patience (*kṣānti*),
this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattvas.
The commentary explains:
To know that all phenomena are without self and thereby achieve patience (*kṣānti*) is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
which is called the cause of wisdom for the manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This Bodhisattva’s merit surpasses that obtained by the preceding Bodhisattvas.
That is to say, the first five perfections are called the causes of merit because they produce the retribution of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
the tenth [perfection] is for the purpose of elucidating the fruits of the true body (*dharmakāya*) and the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
As the sutra says: "If there were someone who said that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down..."
This person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this?
One who comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is therefore called a Tathāgata.
The commentary states:
Phrases such as "coming" and "going" clarify the fruit of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body);
likewise, phrases such as "there is no going" clarify the *dharmakāya* (true body).
Regarding the essential purport of the Second Dhyāna Sūtra:
this sūtra clarifies wisdom above all,
and thus takes Prajñā as its primary tenet.
However, there are three differences regarding Prajñā:
first, the Real Aspect (lakṣaṇa);
second, Contemplative Insight (pratyavekṣaṇā).
Three characters.
These three meanings encompass all forms of wisdom (*prajñā*);
the true mark (*dharmatā*) reveals the objective realm of *prajñā*.
Contemplative observation reveals the essence of prajñā;
written words are the means by which prajñā is expressed.
Since there can be no realization of the ultimate meaning without such expression, [words are necessary].
The characters receive the name "wisdom," for there is no realm that cannot serve to designate the Truth; thus,
their actual nature accords with the stage of Prajñā.
Thus we know that while it is conventionally said that wisdom encompasses both principle and phenomena,
to speak of the ultimate reality, the essence is solely contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This contemplative insight is precisely the meaning of this sutra.
The Vajra possesses the functional method of cutting and severing; that this is the point where the characteristics and the essence are clarified is precisely what is meant here.
Now, regarding the *prajñā* of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is explained through six meanings according to the *Vyūharāja-śāstra*.
First, it has wisdom as its intrinsic nature,
because it is able to correctly discern all phenomena.
Second, it has meditative concentration as its cause.
Because they arise based on meditative concentration (samādhi),
the third has liberation as its fruit,
since one attains liberation from defiled phenomena (kliṣṭadharma).
Fourth, it takes explaining with life as its activity.
This is because a bodhisattva takes wisdom as their life and taking correct explanation as their activity.
5. It is characterized by preeminence as its corresponding attribute, because it is preeminent among all phenomena.
6. It is categorized into three types.
This refers to the mundane, the supramundane, and the great supramundane.
Regarding the third category, the assemblies of the vidyāsthānas:
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, these are taught in four locations across sixteen assemblies.
Regarding the four locations:
the first is on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha;
the second is at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.
The third was in the Maṇiratnagarbha Hall of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the fourth was by the Śarabhañjaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove Garden at Rājagṛha.
Regarding what are called the sixteen assemblies:
It is exactly as stated there.
Question:
Among the four locations [of this sūtra], at which location should it be said to be taught?
In which of the sixteen assemblies was it taught?
Answer:
Among the four locations, it was taught at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
This is the ninth discourse within the sixteen assemblies.
Fourth, the account of the translator:
this sutra has undergone a total of six translations throughout its history.
The first was translated during the Later Qin period by the Dharma Master Kumārajīva in Chang’an;
the text states "Śrāvastī.
The second was translated during the Later Wei period by the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master Bodhiruci in Luoyang.
The text states "Bhagavān.
This includes a three-fascicle translation of Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s commentary and a ten-fascicle record by Vajrasena.
The third was translated at Guangzhou by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha during the Chen and Liang dynasties.
The text states "Jeta’s Grove" and includes the original record in four fascicles.
The fourth [fascicle] is the *Vajracchedikā*, translated during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
He also translated two fascicles of the treatises of Asanga.
Fifth is the *Vajracchedikā*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;
there is also the *Śrīguṇaratnasaṃcaya-gāthā* in two fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Sūryavarman.
The sixth week was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.
The text states that the Buddha, the Bhagavat, was in the great city of Yaśovatī,
and he also retranslated three fascicles of Vasubandhu’s commentary.
As noted above, while the general substance of these various editions is largely the same,
because the Chinese text varies between being concise and expansive,
those who read and uphold them have come to look toward the Qin translation with particular reverence.
Among those who study the doctrines, most follow the Wei edition.
That which I now explain is precisely the Qin edition of the sutra translated by Master Kumārajīva.
Fifth, regarding the correct explanation of the meaning of the text,
there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the title of the scripture.
The second section explains the meaning through an analysis of the text.
First, regarding the interpretation of the title:
"Vajra" in the scripture refers to the jewel that serves as the metaphor.
Because it is the hardest among metals, it is called "vajra.
This jewel possesses many distinct types of substances;
for now, we shall briefly take its two meanings of hardness and sharpness.
"Solidity" refers to its essence, while "sharpness" refers to its function.
Because its essence is solid, things cannot destroy it;
because its function is sharp, it is able to crush all things.
Prajñā is the dharma that serves as the metaphor.
In the Sanskrit language, prajñā is translated here as "pure wisdom."
It is also called signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*).
Because these three types of knowledge are themselves termed "insight" (*prajñā*),
such wisdom is identical to that vajra.
*Pāra* is a Sanskrit term;
here it is translated as "shore.
There are two kinds of shores.
First, this shore;
second, the other shore.
"Mitra" is a Sanskrit term.
This is called "being able to reach," and it is also called "being able to leave.
One takes the birth-and-death of the triple world as this shore.
Bodhi and nirvāṇa constitute the far shore;
the two obstacles and afflictions constitute the middle current; and the wondrous function of prajñā serves as the boat and raft.
Therefore, those who resolve their minds for enlightenment board the boat of wondrous function and abandon the shore of saṃsāra.
To cross the ocean of afflictions and ascend the mountain of nirvāṇa—
therefore it is called a *pāramitā*.
As for "sūtra," it is so named because it pierces through and upholds its intended meaning.
This immediately penetrates the meanings that ought to be explained and sustains those beings to be converted:
the seven characters above are that which is expressed (*vācya*),
while the single character below is that which expresses (*vācaka*).
Because it expresses both the signifier and the signified,
as well as the dharma and its analogies, it is titled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The explanation of the title is hereby concluded.
From this point onward, the scriptural text is divided into sections. The Sūtra states:

"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. Following the precedent established by Master Dao’an, all sūtras—whether large or small—are divided into three parts.
That is to say, there are the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination.
Now, this sutra is likewise divided into three parts;
the first is called the introductory section (nidāna).
From "At that time, the Elder Subhūti... down to "...should contemplate in this manner" constitutes the Main Body (zhèngzōngfēn).
From the subsequent section "After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra... down to "...faithfully received and practiced it" [constitutes the Conclusion].
This is the section on circulation (parīndanā).
Within the initial section on the introduction (nidāna), it is further divided into two parts;
the first is called the section on the introduction for establishing faith (saddhā-deśanā-nidāna).

The latter part, titled "The Introduction on the Arousing [of the Resolve]," is divided into seven sections based on the *Prajñā* commentary by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha within the preceding "Introduction on the Certification of Faith."
"Thus it is" (*iti*) marks the Dharma as it was heard.
Ānanda said that because the sūtras spoken by the Buddha accord with all phenomena (*dharmas*), they are called "thus-ness" (*tathatā*).
Because these phenomena accord with principle and are not erroneous, they are termed "correct" (*iti*).
Second, "I" refers to the person who is able to hear;
it designates the Dharma-transmitting disciple, the Bhikṣu Ānanda, as a provisional entity composed of the five aggregates.
Third, "hearing" means personally receiving the spoken words.
This means that when the faculty of the ear gives rise to consciousness to hear and receive, it is called "hearing.
Regarding "at one time" (ekasamaya), this clarifies that the Dharma heard is perfectly suited to the timing and circumstances;
that is, the speaker and the listener meet together, neither before nor after, which is termed "at one time."
The "Five Buddhas" indicate the teachers who preach.
*Buddha* in the Sanskrit language means "the Awakened One."
One is called a Buddha because they possess the wisdom of both the ultimate and the conventional, and have fulfilled their own and others' awakening.
Regarding the phrase "in Śrāvastī and so forth," this indicates the location where the teaching was spoken.
The place where he dwelt while traveling to transform beings was designated as "In.
Śrāvastī means "Hearing Things" (聞物).
Jeta’s Grove refers to the trees donated by Prince Jeta.
This person, known as Jayasena,
was the crown prince of King Prasenajit.
As for the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden:
This was the garden purchased by the elder Sudatta,
who is here called Shan-shi (Good Giver).
He was compassionate within and wealthy without.
He relieved the poor and comforted the widows; his fellow villagers praised him and called him "Giver to the Lonely" (Anāthapiṇḍada).
Because Sudatta covered the garden with gold and Jeta offered the trees, they together established the vihāra.
In this passage, the names of two individuals are mentioned together to identify the name of the monastery;
thus it is called the Jeta Grove and the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
Regarding the phrase "together with a great assembly of bhikṣus":
this clarifies that it was not heard alone.
"Together with" (yù) means shared; "great" (dà) means superior.
These bhikṣus are all great arhats;
they are called "great" because they surpass those still in training (śaikṣa).
As for the term "bhikṣu," it is translated here as "mendicant" (qishi).
Because they maintain a pure livelihood.
As for "the assembly," a gathering of four or more people is called an assembly.
Regarding "together with twelve hundred and fifty people": [this refers to the number of monks].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Uruvilvākāśyapa, together with five hundred disciples;
Gayākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa, each with two hundred and fifty disciples."
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with their disciples numbering two hundred and fifty,
were for the most part emanated śrāvakas who constantly followed the Buddha.
Therefore, they are often listed separately in the sūtras.
"Together" (俱) signifies being in the same place and at the same time;
that is to say, whether it be Ānanda or the Tathāgata.
It was while [the Buddha] was staying with the bhikṣus and the fourfold assembly at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Sūtra:

At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in his robes and taken up his bowl at the hour of eating, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having completed his alms-round through the city in due order, he returned to his original location. From here below, the third section, the Prologue of the Arousing [of the Teaching], is clarified.
The meanings of "initiation" (samutthāna) differ in many ways,
as explained extensively in various sūtras;
however, this present sūtra specifically elucidates wisdom (prajñā).
It takes precepts and meditative concentration as its point of departure.
Within the introductory section on this departure, the text is divided into three parts.
First, it demonstrates that the transformation through precepts clarifies that samādhi has a cause.
Subsequently, it is shown that concentration, which encompasses clarity and wisdom, constitutes the fruit.
This is the opening of the text.
Within the text, there are seven phrases.
First, at that time, the World-Honored One (Bhagavān) was the enlightened Master.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Because he possesses the aforementioned nine titles, he is called the World-Honored One."
"Mealtime" (śikṣā-kāla) refers to the second clarification of the morning transformation.

Since the activities of the hours of *yin* and *mao* have not yet been completed, and the meal of *si* and *wu* has already concluded, one goes on alms-round during the hour of *chen*; therefore, it is called "mealtime."
"Putting on robes and holding the alms bowl" refers to the third [section],
which clarifies the ritual of transformation.
"Putting on robes" refers to wearing the *saṃghāṭī* and other garments when entering royal palaces or villages.
It is also called the "robe for subduing non-Buddhists.
As for the one who holds the bowl, he holds the stone bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings beneath the Bodhi tree;
through the Buddha's supernormal power, these became four such bowls.
According to this, it is one name for the *pramāṇa-bhājana* (measuring vessel).
The World-Honored One donned robes in order to refute the naked heretics (*nirgrantha*).
It was in order to prevent people from offering food with their hands that he carried an alms bowl when entering the great city of Śrāvastī.
The fourth section clarifies the location of the transformation site.
According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions),
the garden was located five or six li south of the city.
Now, going from the outside to the inside is called "entering.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"This city is twelve yojanas in length and breadth."
Because there were nine hundred million householders, it is called "Great.
This fifth section clarifies the deeds of transformation for the mendicants.
As stated in the *Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body*:
The Tathāgata’s transformation body is entirely composed of adamantine, devoid of both the raw and the ripened storehouses; yet,
he now manifests as one who begs for alms,
thereby providing manifold benefits to sentient beings by becoming a field of merit for them.
Just as Mahākāśyapa abandons the wealthy to follow the poor, benefiting the poor rather than the wealthy;
and Subhūti abandons the poor to follow the wealthy, benefiting the wealthy rather than the poor—
the Buddha, out of impartial benefit for all, practices alms-round in successive order.
"Returning to his original place" marks the seventh [section], clarifying the conclusion of the transformation.
There are two locations where the Tathāgata eats:
first, when he accepts an invitation and stays in the home of a layperson.
The second [practice] is to return to one's dwelling after finishing the meal of alms-food without receiving more.
Now, returning to the Jeta Grove corresponds to this second [practice].
This is because, in total, he is content; he does not beg beyond measure; and he knows the proper time, thus returning to his original place.
In the Sūtra,

the passage "having finished eating and put away the robes and bowl" indicates that the second [stage] demonstrates the attainment of wisdom through the concentration of meditative absorption as its fruit.
The text contains three sections:
first, the auxiliary conditions;
second, pure karma.
Third, this section primarily clarifies entering meditative absorption;
it is the beginning of this text.
For external transformation necessarily relies upon robes and alms bowls.

Having first clarified the essential points for wearing and maintaining the robes within the quietude of the monastery, as well as the necessary requisites, they are now collected and set forth in this sutra.
Regarding the phrase "having washed one's feet":
This is the second [aspect of] the purification of bodily action.
The *Xiánjì* (Record of the Immortals) states:
"When the Tathāgata walks, the earth deities transform into flowers to receive his feet."
He remains four finger-widths above the ground for the sake of sentient beings;
he shows his feet becoming soiled while traveling on the road to teach the entry into meditative concentration;
and he demonstrates the purification of bodily action.
In the sutra,
"having spread his seat and sat down" refers to the third section,
which correctly clarifies the expedient means for entering meditative concentration.
First, he spreads out his seat,
which is the *niṣīdana*— here translated as "spreading mat.
The phrase "sits down" precisely clarifies that he enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The above concludes the explanation of the introductory section (*nidāna*). Sūtra:

At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverent salutation. From this point downward is the second part, which elucidates the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*).
In this context, many people roughly divide [the text] into two cycles:
the first clarifies the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), and the second, beginning with "How so? (*kathaṃ ca*), clarifies the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*).
Now, examining the logic and phrasing, it appears this is not the case; for in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, within the section on "Severing Doubts," it is explained by the author himself:
"From here onwards, it clarifies that all sūtras manifest [the teaching] in order to sever the arising of doubt."
Since it has already been stated that all-knowing wisdom is not something separate, we shall now divide the text of the main body of the teaching into four sections.
First: Subhūti’s Request.
First, the Tathāgata’s praise and approval;
second, Subhūti’s delight in hearing;
third, the Tathāgata’s correct response; and fourth, [the subsequent teaching].
This is the beginning of the text.
The text further consists of three parts.
First, the identification and enumeration of those who make the request.
Second is the praise of the Buddha’s virtue of transformation;
third is the formal proclamation of the request for teaching.
This is the beginning of that [third section].
What is called "time" refers to the time for inquiring about the Dharma.
What is called "Elder" (sthavira) is a term of respect,
meaning one who possesses the virtues of being senior and aged.
Subhūti is the one who requested the Dharma.
The name Subhūti contains three meanings.

First, at the time of his birth, the room became empty, manifesting the auspicious sign of emptiness; when his parents asked the master about it, he replied, "Only good, only auspicious," and thus he was named Śubhakiṭa (Auspicious).
He is also called Subhūti,
and also known as Kūṭadanta;
either name may be used without error.
"To rise from one's seat within the great assembly" refers to the purpose of inquiring about the Dharma.
Baring the right shoulder is the gesture of showing respect to one's teacher;
placing the right knee on the ground is...
This is the beginning of the inquiry.
"Joining the palms in reverence" means to compose one's demeanor and focus the mind with single-minded attention.
The Sūtra says:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! This is the second praise of the Buddha’s transformative virtue.
Within this passage, there are two parts.
First is the general praise;
second is the specific praise.
This passage is the general [praise].
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"First, the manifestation of supernatural powers is rare;
second, speaking in opposition to their minds is rare."
Third is the rarity of the teaching and transformation.
What is here called "rarity" refers precisely to this third point, the rarity of the teaching and transformation.
The term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) is the tenth title.
Sūtra.
"That the Tathāgata well protects and attends to all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas" is the second distinct praise of his virtues.
The term "Tathāgata" invokes the foremost title of the Buddha.
*Tathatā* (Suchness) is the dharma realized;
*āgata* (come) is the wisdom capable of realizing it.
Because one attains perfect enlightenment through the realization of Suchness by means of this wisdom, one is called a *Tathāgata*.
Regarding the phrase "skillfully protecting and mindful of all bodhisattvas":
for bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature,
the Buddha himself protects and is mindful of them, causing them to accomplish the qualities of a Buddha’s merit and to conform to the Buddha’s own practice of self-benefit.
Furthermore, the method for transforming sentient beings is identical to the Buddha’s altruistic practice.
Regarding the term "entrustment" (*parindanā*):

when the roots of a bodhisattva are not yet mature, the Buddha will entrust them to a bodhisattva whose roots are mature, charging them with the task of teaching and receiving [the dharma], so that those who have already attained the Mahāyāna do not regress and those who have not yet attained it may advance in their cultivation.
Bodhisattvas who have already entered the lineage are said to have mature faculties;
bodhisattvas prior to entering the lineage are said to have immature faculties.
Sūtra.

"Bhagavān, how should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their mind? This is the third section, the formal words of the request.
The term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) identifies the person capable of answering;
"good sons and good daughters" clarifies the persons for whom [the teaching] is intended.
Possessing the faculties such as faith is termed "wholesome.
The phrase "one who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" indicates the specific state of mind that is produced.
"A" means "non-";
"anuttara" means "supreme"; the three names [of the next term] mean "correct."

Taken as a whole, it is called "unsurpassed perfect complete enlightenment.
"Perfect" refers precisely to the wisdom that accords with reality (yathābhūta-jñāna),
while "complete" refers to the wisdom of the full extent of phenomena (yāvadbhāva-jñāna).
Knowing this is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*);
awakening to this is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Because it takes reality as its object, it is called "correct" according to the principle of suchness (*yathābhūta-yukti*).
Because knowledge of things as they are (*yathāvad-jñāna*) takes conventional reality as its object, it is called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*);
because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) eliminates the two types of ignorance, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
and because subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) transcends the realm of eyes and dreams, it is called "awakening" (*buddhi*).
These four wisdoms are the very essence of the fruit of Buddhahood.
If a person resolves their mind to seek this fruit from afar, it is called "generating the bodhicitta.
As for how one should abide and how one should subdue the mind: [the text continues...]
This clarifies the practice requested.

As for the words "Excellent, excellent":

This is as you have described and so forth.

"I shall now explain for you how a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and how they should subdue their minds. This is the third promise to teach.

Sūtra:
The Buddha told Subhūti, "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. From here below begins the fourth section: the Tathāgata’s direct response.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the answer to the question;

begins from the passage: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give gifts in this manner.
The answer to the previously mentioned question, "How should one subdue the mind? follows below that.
This passage is the first response to the preceding question regarding the stages (*vihāra*).
According to the Wei translation of the sutra, it asks:
"In this context, how does a bodhisattva give rise to such a mind?"
Regarding the term "subduing" (降伏) in this [Chinese] original text:
according to the Sanskrit original, it simply means being able to give rise to and being able to deliver sentient beings;
since the sense of "subduing" those who would not otherwise be delivered is already inherent therein.
This is a translation based on the meaning of "subduing.
The text consists of two parts.
First, it generally instructs on subduing [the mind] by demonstrating the arousal of the four types of resolve, beginning with the vast resolve.
Next, regarding the characteristics of the four types of mental activity arising from the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*),
this is the opening passage.
As for the term "Bodhisattva":
"Bodhi" refers to enlightenment,
which is the fruit of Buddhahood that is sought;
"sattva" refers to a being.
These are precisely the sentient beings to be transformed.
It is because these individuals possess wisdom that they are able to seek the fruit of Buddhahood above,
and because they possess compassion that they are able to transform sentient beings below.
"Bodhi" means awakening;
"sattva" means a being; thus one is called a Bodhisattva.
"One should subdue the mind in this way" means:
This refers to subduing the mind of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who do not resolve to deliver sentient beings;
it is precisely the arising of the bodhisattva’s mind to deliver sentient beings.
Sūtra:
"Regarding all categories of sentient beings":
this is the second section, which explains the characteristics of the arising of the four types of mind according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
The text is divided into four parts.
First, the elucidation of the vast mind;
second, the elucidation of the supreme mind;
third, the elucidation of the eternal mind.
Fourth is the non-perverted mind.
Within the section on the vast mind, there are two distinct parts:
first, a general presentation, followed by a detailed exposition.
This is a general summary.
As for the term "vast," it refers to manifesting the mind by way of its objects.
Because its objective range is vast and all-pervasive, the mind is called "extensive.
The phrase "all classes of sentient beings whatsoever" refers collectively to all sentient beings within the four modes of birth and the three realms of existence.
Therefore, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states:
"This is a statement in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the term 'sentient beings' (*sattva*):"
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Within the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), that which arises is called a 'sentient being' (*sattva*).
[Sūtra] says:
Whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation—the latter part of the text clarifies this.
According to the treatise of Asaṅga, these are categorized into three types of inclusion:
first, the inclusion of taking birth.
Second is inclusion by way of support;
third is inclusion by way of object.
This is the first [category], inclusion by way of birth.
There are four different modes of birth.
That which is born from a shell is called egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).
That which emerges from being contained within is called womb-born (*jarāyuja*).
That which arises through the moisture of conditions is termed "moisture";
that which suddenly comes into existence where there was none is termed "transformation.
These four types encompass all sentient beings without exception.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva summarizes this as his vow.
The Sūtra says:
"Whether there is form or whether there is no form. The second [phrase] refers to the reliance upon this body.
If they possess form,
it refers to the two realms of desire and form, because they possess a physical body;
if they are formless, it refers to the formless realm.
This means that because sentient beings in the four higher formless realms lack physical form,
these two [realms] also encompass all sentient beings. Therefore,
the Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to transcend the three realms in their entirety.
Sūtra:
"Whether with perception, or without perception, or with neither perception nor non-perception"—this is the designation for the third stage.
Perception is that which grasps the object.
Because this object of apprehension is conceived as a clearly manifest object,
it is said to be included within the "sphere" (viṣaya).
If there is such a conception, [it is so].
This means that among the sentient beings from the Sphere of Nothingness downward, with the exception of the single class of non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*),
all others possess coarse perception and grasp coarse objects;
as for those who are non-percipient:
This refers to the fact that within the four dhyānas, the single realm of non-perception (asaṃjñika) entirely lacks a perceiving mind that grasps objects.
As for "neither with perception nor without perception," this refers to the single stage of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra);
because its coarse perception is absent, it is called "neither with perception," and because subtle perception still exists, it is called "nor without perception."
Regarding the phrase "neither with perception nor without perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*):
if the character *ruò* (若) were omitted, or if the subsequent *ruò* were retained, it would not constitute a single stage (*bhūmi*).
These three [stages] likewise encompass all sentient beings without exception.
Sūtra:

"I cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. This second [section] clarifies the first resolve (*prathama-citta*), meaning that he causes sentient beings to attain the supreme bliss of Great *Nirvāṇa*.
However, those vast vows thus generated by that bodhisattva are his resolve.
To bring about ultimate and eternal bliss for sentient beings is called the "first mind.

the ten thousand practices and six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) of the Bodhisattva constitute the source of their vows;
among these perfections, the meaning of *dāna* comprehensively encompasses them all.
Therefore, by citing this single title, all six gates are encompassed:
namely, the *dānapāramitā* is called the "gift of material sustenance," while the *śīlapāramitā* and *kṣāntipāramitā* are called the "gift of fearlessness."
This means that upholding the precepts, practicing patience, and bestowing fearlessness upon others constitute the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Furthermore, diligence (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are also termed the giving of the Dharma;
it is through diligence that one is said to be free from weariness.
By means of meditative concentration, one is able to know the minds of others;
by means of wisdom, one is able to speak in accordance with reality.
As for the statement that "one should practice giving without dwelling on anything regarding phenomena," it means:
One practices without attachment to the reward of karmic fruition.
One should not seek rewards such as offerings, honor, or praise from others.
Sūtra.

This refers to "giving without dwelling on form, and giving without dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena. The third point clarifies the practice of non-dwelling regarding karmic retribution;
that is, not seeking future fruits such as rebirth among humans or devas.
This fruit is called "retribution" because it compensates for the cause;
that is, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and so forth constitute the substance of the future fruit. When one practices this giving, it is termed "attaining retribution.
A Bodhisattva remains detached from these, which is termed "not dwelling in form and so forth."
Sūtra:
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not dwelling upon signs. This is the third answer, responding to the question regarding the subduing of the mind.
According to the Wei translation of the sūtra, it says:
"One does not dwell upon the perception of signs.

first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; fourth, the analogy; fifth, the application; and sixth, the exhortation.

If the dual grasping of the characteristics and the conceptualization has not yet been extinguished,
one who seeks true emptiness will instead produce further outflows.
Therefore, because the bodhisattva eliminates false conceptualization and purifies the three spheres,
he further demonstrates subjugation through the gateway of giving.
To say "not dwelling on the perception of signs" means:

As for the question in the sutra, "For what reason? [it is as follows].

The reason for this is that all merits such as giving arise from mental conceptions.

"If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, the resulting merit is inconceivable. This is the third explanation.
Dwelling on signs results in outflowing (sāsrava) retribution, which is finite; by not dwelling [on signs], one attains the non-outflowing (anāsrava).
"The mass of merit is immeasurable. Sūtra:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured? This is the fourth analogy.

the realm of space is not the ten directions;

"Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? This second section extensively cites the nine directions.

the names and meanings are as explained above.

"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? From this point downward is the second major section, which clarifies the severing of doubts.

specifically, there are thirty-two doubts.
Although the treatise does not explicitly enumerate them, they lack individual headings.
Now, drawing upon the purport of the treatise, I shall briefly establish a name for this.

how does one practice giving for the sake of the Buddha’s bodhi?
To sever this doubt, there are six sections of the sūtra text.

and sixth, the conclusion. This is the first part, the question:
"Is it possible to perceive the true Dharma-body by means of the three characteristics of conditioned form—namely, arising, abiding, and changing?"
[Sūtra]:
"No, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the marks of his body.
This is the second answer, intended to prevent doubt.
To falsely give rise to conceptual discrimination and, grasping at conditioned characteristics, claim to see the Dharmakāya—
for this reason, the response in the Sūtra states in general that it is "impossible. Sūtra:
Why is this? This is the third inquiry.

We currently observe that the Tathāgata was born in a royal palace, attained parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees, remained in the world for eighty years, and possessed a body perfected with the thirty-two marks.
Why is it said that one cannot see [the Tathāgata] by means of physical marks?

"The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are themselves not physical marks. This is the fourth explanation.
The physical marks are false appearances; the Dharma-body is called the true mark.
False appearances are not the Dharma-body; the name of the mark is itself no mark.
Sūtra.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All that has marks is entirely illusory.
This is the fifth exposition.
It is because having marks is deceptive and does not accord with reality.
The scripture says: "All marks whatsoever are empty and false.
If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. This is the sixth fulfillment.
If one perceives that conditioned phenomena are illusory in nature and not the unconditioned, true nature,
this very realization of the Dharmakāya is called "seeing the Buddha."
Therefore, it is said that one "sees the Tathāgata immediately.

In the Sūtra, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these, will give rise to true faith? From this point downward, the third doubt is resolved.

"Previously, based on the *pāramitās*, it was taught that one should practice without dwelling."
Regarding the gift, the profound meaning of the cause has been explained;
regarding the Tathāgata, who is not of a conditioned nature, the profound meaning of the fruit has been explained.
If this were so, people in the future evil age would not give rise to faith.
How is it that the "not empty" is taught?

first, Subhūti’s inquiry.

this is the first question.
The word "poha" (頗) signifies "capable."
Regarding such profound sutras, while there are those capable of faith during the present True Dharma,
will there be those in the future, the era of evil people, who can give rise to true faith? Sutra.
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do not speak thus. This is the second part, the Tathāgata’s correct response.
Within this passage there are two sections:
first, the reprimand, and second, the instruction.
This is the first censure.
The reason for this censure is merely to quell their doubts.
[The] Sūtra [says]:
"In the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa" refers to the subsequent teaching through texts.
These texts are further divided into two types:
first, the general teaching, and second, the specific teaching.
In total, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the timing;
second, clarifying the merit.
Third, the signs of faith.
This first section clarifies the period of faith.
According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, five kinds of firmness are taught.
During the first five hundred years, liberation will be firm;
during the next five hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm;
during the subsequent five hundred years, extensive learning will be firm.
The next five hundred years were characterized by the firm establishment of merit;
the subsequent five hundred years were characterized by the firm establishment of strife.
What is now referred to as "the final five hundred years" refers to this latter period.
This corresponds precisely to the fifth five-hundred-year period.
During this degenerate age, there will be those capable of giving rise to faith.
Sūtra.
"Those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit" refers to the second [section], which clarifies their illustrious virtue.
According to the Wei edition of the sutra, "wisdom" is added here; this current version is abbreviated.
As for the term "upholding the precepts," it means the cessation and extinction of all evils.
Merit refers to the cultivation of various samādhis;
wisdom refers to conformity with the two kinds of emptiness.
One must necessarily possess these three trainings.
Only then can genuine faith arise.
Question:
Are not the first five perfections collectively termed "merit" (puṇya)?
How do we know that this meaning applies exclusively to the gate of meditative concentration?
Answer:
To discuss it comprehensively, it encompasses the preceding five [gates].
One should focus on excelling specifically in the training of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*),
because within the excellence of concentration one can accumulate merit and bring about the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and matters of peace and happiness.
In this sūtra,
those who are able to give rise to faith in these words and take them as true—
this is the third [section], clarifying the characteristic of clarity.
"Regarding these chapters and verses" refers to the profound teaching on cause and effect.
"Able to give rise to faith" means...
This refers to a person who is endowed with virtue.
To take this as the reality is precisely to clearly believe in the characteristic of appearance.
Since faith is thus complete,
how could this exposition be in vain? Thus says the Sūtra:

It should be known that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but has planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Buddhas.
The subsequent text concerns the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
Within it, there are two parts;
the first clarifies the cultivation of merit.
The subsequent section clarifies the cultivation of wisdom;
this is the beginning of that text.
Within it, there are four parts.
First, clarifying the cause of faith;
second, clarifying the essence of faith;
third, clarifying the conditions for faith.
The fourth clarifies the accumulation of the fruit;
this is precisely the first cause of faith.
Regarding the statement, "not under one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas":
"Clarifying that they are not few and are no different from those at the initial stage" refers to those who have already been with immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas;
"manifesting that they have already received many predictions and their faculties are matured" refers to those who have planted various roots of goodness.
This refers to burning incense, scattering flowers, invoking the name [of the Buddha], and praising his virtues within the field of the Buddha,
thereby planting the three kinds of wholesome roots, such as non-attachment. Sūtra:
"Those who hear these phrases and even give rise to pure faith for a single moment"—
this second section clarifies the essence of faith.
"Even giving rise to pure faith for a single moment."
"One thought-moment" (*ekacitta*) refers to the pure mental disposition (*cittāśaya*) of a single *kṣaṇa*.
Since faith has purity of mind as its essential nature, it is called "pure faith.
[The Sūtra says:]
"Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings. This is the third clear exposition on the condition [for faith].
Because they are known and seen by the Buddha, their faith does not regress.
Question:
What is the distinction between the two types, knowledge and vision?
Answer:
The fleshly eye is seeing but not knowing;
inferential knowledge is knowing but not seeing;
the knowledge of aspiration is both knowing and seeing.
Because it differs from the fleshly eye, it is said that he "knows";
because it differs from inferential cognition, it is said that he "sees.
Therefore, it is said that he "fully knows and fully sees."
Because the Buddha possesses knowledge and vision,
if there is anyone who desires to receive offerings and respect,
they may praise themselves as already possessing meritorious qualities such as the observance of precepts.
That person cannot explain it because this person knows it for himself.
Sūtra:
"One obtains such immeasurable merit. This fourth [section] clearly explains the fruit.

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
"That is to say, for a person of wisdom..."
By generating great faith in the supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna, one attains three kinds of fruits:

second, the attainment of the fruit of great merit because merit increases.
Third, because the merit of attaining the fruit of great enlightenment is peerless, and because it constitutes the great essence of a Buddha.
Sūtra: "For what reason? From here on, the subsequent text explains the cultivation of wisdom.
The text consists of three parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the reaffirmation; and third, the differentiation of distinctions.
Within the first part, there are again two sections.
First there is the interrogation, followed by the explanation;
this passage constitutes the interrogation.
The intent of the interrogation is as follows:
Having cultivated merit and thereby generated pure faith,
what is the further purpose of explaining the cultivation of wisdom?
The Sūtra says:
"These sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span. This is the explanation found in the subsequent text.
Herein there are two parts;
first is the explanation of being free from the mark of a self.
The following explains the departure from the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
This is the beginning of that section.
Question:
The four characteristics of these [clinging aggregates] are collectively termed "self-clinging" (ātma-grāha).
What is the distinction for establishing these four names?
Answer:
Not observing the distinctions between the three periods of time, one grasps them collectively as a self;
this is called the characteristic of self (ātman-lakṣaṇa).
One calculates that the present aggregates continue [into the future].
The former meaning is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*);

Considering the present aggregates and destinies,
the latter six are designated as the characteristics of humans;
due to these distinctions, they are called four types.
The Sūtra states:
"There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. The subsequent text provides a separate explanation regarding the departure from the marks of dharmas.
According to the Wei translation of the Sūtra, there are four phrases.
In this context, there are only two points:
that there is no characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) avoids the fault of reification (samāropa),
